title: Fast Exponentiation
tagline: Compute aⁿ (mod m) in O(log n) by squaring — the workhorse of modular math.

intuition.analogy: To compute a¹⁶ you don't multiply a sixteen times. You square: a→a²→a⁴→a⁸→a¹⁶ — just four multiplications. Any exponent is built from these power-of-two squares according to its binary digits.
paragraphs: Binary (fast) exponentiation computes aⁿ using the binary representation of n. Each bit of n corresponds to a successive square of a; you multiply the result by the current square only where the bit is 1.

This turns O(n) multiplications into O(log n). Combined with a modulus, modular exponentiation is the backbone of cryptography (RSA), modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem, and counting problems under a prime modulus.
The same square-and-combine idea generalises to matrix exponentiation — computing the n-th Fibonacci number or linear-recurrence terms in O(log n) by raising a transition matrix to the n-th power.
intuition.keyIdea: Square the base while halving the exponent; multiply into the result only on set bits of n.

steps.title: Initialise
steps.detail: result = 1; base = a mod m; exponent = n.

steps.title: Process bits
steps.detail: While n > 0: if n is odd, result = result · base mod m; then base = base · base mod m and n >>= 1.

steps.title: Return
steps.detail: result holds aⁿ mod m after log n iterations.

complexity.timeReason: The exponent halves each iteration, so there are ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 steps.

pitfalls: Overflow: use 64-bit (or 128-bit / __int128) for the products before taking mod.
Fermat inverse a^(m−2) mod m only works when m is prime and a is not a multiple of m.
0^0 conventions vary — handle if your problem cares.

dryRun.clickMoment: The exponent 13 = 8+4+1, exactly its set bits. The result only absorbs the squares at those bit positions (a¹·a⁴·a⁸ = a¹³) — binary made the exponent additive.

problems.title: Pow(x, n)
problems.statement: Implement double power with integer exponent.

approach: Binary exponentiation: square the base and halve the exponent, multiplying into the result when the current bit is set.
For negative n, compute the positive power and take the reciprocal. O(log n).

problems.title: Super Pow
problems.statement: Compute a^b mod 1337 where b is a huge array of digits.

approach: The exponent is a huge number given as a digit array, so apply the rule a^(10·q + d) = (a^q)^10 · a^d, processing digits left to right.
Keep everything modulo 1337 using fast exponentiation for the ^10 and ^d steps.

problems.title: Fibonacci via Matrix Power
problems.statement: Compute the n-th Fibonacci number in O(log n).

approach: Fibonacci satisfies [[1,1],[1,0]]^n = [[F(n+1),F(n)],[F(n),F(n-1)]]. Raise the matrix by fast exponentiation.
Each multiply is 2×2; O(log n) multiplications give F(n) modulo a prime.

problems.title: Count Good Numbers
problems.statement: Count digit strings under modular rules.
problems.hint: Closed form with modular fast power.

approach: Even indices (0-based) must hold an even digit (0,2,4,6,8 → 5 choices); odd indices must hold a prime digit (2,3,5,7 → 4 choices).
There are ceil(n/2) even positions and floor(n/2) odd positions, so the answer is 5^ceil(n/2) · 4^floor(n/2) mod 1e9+7 via fast power.

problems.title: Modular Inverse (Fermat)
problems.statement: Compute inverses under a prime modulus.
problems.hint: a^(p−2) mod p via fast power.

approach: When the modulus p is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives a^(p-1) ≡ 1, so the inverse of a is a^(p-2) mod p.
